doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Spinning Wheel intro, arranging, and the Band's Lonesome Suzie
summary: Hearing charts back, the sharp nine in Spinning Wheel, and comparing his arrangement with the Band's Lonesome Suzie.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Getting back to your writing charts, when you’d bring a chart to the band and read it down, did it usually come out the way —
I’m glad you asked me that.
Because this was long before Finale or something, that you could hear something back.

No. The thing that I was going to mention at the clinic too, to these young rock & rollers or whatever kind of music. Do what inspires you. The intro on “Spinning Wheel” [scats] I’m wondering, is that okay for pop music? That was unheard of, to have a sharp nine chord. Only one other group [sings] “I love you baby” and what’s that group? Frankie Valli?

In the 1950s they used sharp 9, it was a sharp nine chord I think. But it came out so smooth. I don’t think it was ever used in rock & roll before. And I did and I’m going is this okay with most of what I wrote. Totally naïve, and it became a number two. So you just follow your heart. And whenever I’ve tried to copy too much, do what I think is — it doesn’t happen. And then I do stuff that no one else has done. So getting back to your question, I was just thinking about this because I want to speak to these kids for this clinic in a couple of days. And we’re going to talk about “Spinning Wheel” and other, what makes a good arrangement. So an arrangement I wrote of the Band, the group the Band, Robbie Robertson and Michael — Richard Manuel. He wrote “Lonesome Suzie.” I don’t know if you ever heard it.
Oh yeah, it’s one of my favorites.

He sings it beautifully, it’s very simple, I want to compare the two. It’s not that Fred’s arrangement is better, I just want them to hear what people do to color an arrangement or not color it. And I liken it to a coloring book, a black and white coloring book for kids. Look, you can keep the picture of the duck the same with the little bits of water, or you can color in the water or the grass green or make it yellowish or make the duck lighter. Whatever color. So that’s like brass or strings or whatever you know. So that’s kind of what an arranger does, and also you try to enhance.
